How many licks does it actually take to get to the center of a tootsie pop?

Back in highschool a buddy of mine tried this.

The problem is defining and controlling your variables.

For example, defining what a lick is, and maintaining consistent licks. If he stuck out his tounge and pulled the lollipop 5cm down the length of his tongue in 1 second after his mouth was good and moist (not dry from sticking out his tounge for 30 minutes), I think that would be a proper lick. But that would mean closing his mouth and sloshing around some spit between each lick, but that was too time consuming for the task to be completed during lunch and 6th period biology, so we settled for a faster, but far less scientific method. He stuck out his tounge and rubbed the pop in about 1.5cm pulls along his tounge, maybe 100 times a minute, then closed his mouth when his jaw got fatigued.

But now we have the question of how to hold the lollipop. If we rotate it constantly, we can keep a more circular form and constantly be licking tangential to the lollipop, thus hitting a very small patch of the actual lollipop each time. But if start of one side and lick all the way through, when you're halfway through, you'll be getting a huge cross sectional area of the lollipop contacting your tounge. We only realized this was a factor halfway through the lollipop, and decided not to account for it.

Anyway, our experiment came out to about 1500 licks, but the accuracy of that number could vary wildly when you start controlling the variables.

So I guess, you should conduct your own experiment and report back.

I'm done. I will just buy cheap ass variants and replace it more often. I hate everything about doing that - the time, the environmental impact, the hassle. But if it's what makes more sense financially, then that's what I'll give up and do.

The problem is this type of thing has a knock on effect. You are basically wiping the value of commodities. It's the type of thing that causes less liquidity in the system, which can lead to recession. It's another nail in coffin. If the consumer wants cheaper goods, then the quality is going drop. It's a downward cycle that's self perpetuating, and good for no one in the long run. The consumer might save a dollar on q-tips in the short term, but will lose long term.

It definitely sucks, but what are we to do? This kind of thing is being driven by companies like Walmart. They tell vendors that they must drop the price of an item by X% to keep it in their store. Now the vendor has to decide - do I maintain the quality of my product and fire nearly half of my people to stay in business, or do I compromise on quality to meet this target and keep paying my employees?
